claim: Cyanobacteria were responsible for the oxygenation of the ancient atmosphere
source: Cyanobacteria were responsible for the oxygenation of the ancient atmosphere
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bekker et al., 2004 in the abstract and introduction, representing established scientific knowledge

claim: The evolution of Cyanobacteria is enigmatic, as relatives have not been characterized
source: however, the evolution of this phylum is enigmatic, as relatives have not been characterized
evidence: This statement is made in the abstract and represents the knowledge gap that motivated the study

claim: Complete genomes were obtained for members of a new candidate phylum sibling to Cyanobacteria from human fecal and subsurface aquifer metagenomic samples
source: Here we use whole genome reconstruction of human fecal and subsurface aquifer metagenomic samples to obtain complete genomes for members of a new candidate phylum sibling to Cyanobacteria
evidence: This is supported by the genomic data presented in Tables 1 and 2, showing genome assembly statistics

claim: The new candidate phylum sibling to Cyanobacteria is designated 'Melainabacteria'
source: for which we propose the designation 'Melainabacteria'
evidence: This is a nomenclatural proposal made by the authors based on their phylogenetic analyses

claim: The ancestors to both Melainabacteria and Cyanobacteria lineages were non-photosynthetic
source: Metabolic analysis suggests that the ancestors to both lineages were non-photosynthetic, anaerobic, motile, and obligately fermentative
evidence: This is inferred from metabolic reconstruction showing absence of photosynthetic genes in Melainabacteria genomes

claim: The ancestors to both Melainabacteria and Cyanobacteria lineages were anaerobic
source: Metabolic analysis suggests that the ancestors to both lineages were non-photosynthetic, anaerobic, motile, and obligately fermentative
evidence: This is inferred from metabolic reconstruction showing fermentative metabolism in Melainabacteria

claim: The ancestors to both Melainabacteria and Cyanobacteria lineages were motile
source: Metabolic analysis suggests that the ancestors to both lineages were non-photosynthetic, anaerobic, motile, and obligately fermentative
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of flagellar genes in Melainabacteria genomes

claim: The ancestors to both Melainabacteria and Cyanobacteria lineages were obligately fermentative
source: Metabolic analysis suggests that the ancestors to both lineages were non-photosynthetic, anaerobic, motile, and obligately fermentative
evidence: This is inferred from metabolic reconstruction showing fermentative pathways in Melainabacteria

claim: Cyanobacterial light sensing may have been facilitated by regulators present in the ancestor of Cyanobacteria and Melainabacteria lineages
source: Cyanobacterial light sensing may have been facilitated by regulators present in the ancestor of these lineages
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of light response regulator homologs (RpaA, RpaB, NblS) in Melainabacteria genomes

claim: The subsurface organism has the capacity for nitrogen fixation using a nitrogenase distinct from that in Cyanobacteria
source: The subsurface organism has the capacity for nitrogen fixation using a nitrogenase distinct from that in Cyanobacteria, suggesting nitrogen fixation evolved separately in the two lineages
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis of nifH genes showing ACD20 clusters with group III nitrogenases, not with cyanobacterial group I nitrogenases

claim: Nitrogen fixation evolved separately in Melainabacteria and Cyanobacteria lineages
source: The subsurface organism has the capacity for nitrogen fixation using a nitrogenase distinct from that in Cyanobacteria, suggesting nitrogen fixation evolved separately in the two lineages
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distinctness of nitrogenase genes in the two lineages

claim: Cyanobacteria split from Melainabacteria prior to or due to the acquisition of oxygenic photosynthesis
source: We hypothesize that Cyanobacteria split from Melainabacteria prior or due to the acquisition of oxygenic photosynthesis
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the absence of photosynthetic genes in Melainabacteria

claim: Melainabacteria remained in anoxic zones and differentiated by niche adaptation, including for symbiosis in the mammalian gut
source: Melainabacteria remained in anoxic zones and differentiated by niche adaptation, including for symbiosis in the mammalian gut
evidence: This is inferred from the distribution of Melainabacteria in anoxic environments and gut habitats, and their anaerobic metabolism

claim: Cyanobacteria comprise the sole lineage known to have innovated the production of oxygen as a byproduct of photosynthesis
source: Cyanobacteria are presumed responsible for this geochemical revolution, as they comprise the sole lineage known to have innovated the production of oxygen as a byproduct of photosynthesis (Mulkidjanian et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mulkidjanian et al., 2006 and represents established scientific knowledge

claim: Nitrogen fixation by Cyanobacteria is central to the Earth's nitrogen cycle
source: Further, nitrogen fixation by Cyanobacteria is central to the Earth's nitrogen cycle (Vitousek et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vitousek et al., 2002

claim: Cyanobacteria are inferred to be one of the earliest branching bacterial lineages
source: Cyanobacteria are inferred to be one of the earliest branching bacterial lineages (Altermann and Kazmierczak, 2003; Bekker et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Altermann and Kazmierczak, 2003 and Bekker et al., 2004

claim: Cyanobacteria became the chloroplasts of plants via endosymbiosis
source: Via endosymbiosis, Cyanobacteria became the chloroplasts of plants (Sagan, 1967)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sagan, 1967 and represents established scientific knowledge

claim: No related taxa to Cyanobacteria, from which a common ancestor could be inferred, have been described
source: The evolutionary history of the Cyanobacteria phylum is only partially resolved: no related taxa, from which a common ancestor could be inferred, have been described
evidence: This represents the knowledge gap prior to this study

claim: Recent culture-independent 16S rRNA gene surveys have revealed a novel clade sibling and basal to Cyanobacteria
source: However, recent culture-independent 16S rRNA gene surveys of microbial communities have revealed a novel clade sibling and basal to Cyanobacteria (Ley et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ley et al., 2005

claim: Organisms related to Cyanobacteria in the gut are widely shared across individuals
source: The presence of organisms related to Cyanobacteria in the gut is notable because they are widely shared across individuals (Consortium HMP, 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citation to the Human Microbiome Project Consortium, 2012

claim: Members of the Cyanobacteria-related group can comprise up to 20% of the total sequences recovered from stool
source: where members of this group can comprise up to 20% of the total sequences recovered from stool (Dethlefsen and Relman, 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dethlefsen and Relman, 2011

claim: Cyanobacteria-related organisms are shared across various mammalian species
source: as well as shared across various mammalian species (Ley et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ley et al., 2008

claim: It has been assumed that Cyanobacteria-related sequences in the gut represent genomic material derived from ingestion of chloroplasts or Cyanobacterial cells
source: As Cyanobacteria are photosynthetic organisms, it has been assumed that these sequences represent genomic material derived from ingestion of chloroplasts or Cyanobacterial cells (Turnbaugh et al., 2009; Koenig et al., 2011; Consortium HMP, 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Turnbaugh et al., 2009; Koenig et al., 2011; Consortium HMP, 2012

claim: Related bacteria deep-branching from Cyanobacteria have been detected in water and other anoxic environments including sediments
source: Related bacteria deep-branching from the Cyanobacteria have also been detected in water and other anoxic environments including sediments (Ley et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ley et al., 2005

claim: The water-soil-sediment-derived clade is distinct from the gut-derived clade of Cyanobacteria-related bacteria
source: An earlier phylogenetic reconstruction based on full-length 16S rRNA gene sequences indicated that this water-soil-sediment-derived clade is distinct from that made up entirely of gut-derived sequences (Ley et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ley et al., 2005

claim: Metagenomes were generated from three fecal samples obtained from three healthy adult humans
source: We generated metagenomes from three fecal samples obtained from three healthy adult humans (termed A, B, and C; Table 1)
evidence: This describes the experimental data generation

claim: Genome fragments from an organism deeply branching with respect to Cyanobacteria were identified in a subsurface aquifer metagenomic dataset
source: In addition, we identified genome fragments that derived from an organism deeply branching with respect to Cyanobacteria in a microbial community metagenomic dataset from a subsurface aquifer (Wrighton et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wrighton et al., 2012 and represents data analysis

claim: The bacterial communities of human fecal samples A, B, and C are predominantly composed of members of the Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes
source: The bacterial communities of human fecal samples A, B, and C are typical of human fecal microbiota, as they are predominantly composed of members of the Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes, with a few other phyla represented (Figure 1A–C) (Consortium HMP, 2012)
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1A-C showing community composition and citation to HMP Consortium, 2012

claim: The subsurface sample has a greater phylum-level phylogenetic diversity with the most abundant members belonging to Proteobacteria and the candidate phyla OD1 and OP11
source: The subsurface sample, on the other hand, has a greater phylum-level phylogenetic diversity with the most abundant members belonging to Proteobacteria and the candidate phyla OD1 and OP11 (Figure 1D)
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1D showing community composition

claim: The abundances of genomes from the Cyanobacteria sibling clade were less than 5% of the total community in both human fecal and subsurface samples
source: For both sample types, the abundances of genomes from the Cyanobacteria sibling clade were less than 5% of the total community
evidence: This is supported by the abundance data in Table 1

claim: Two genomes were recovered from sample B (MEL.B1, MEL.B2)
source: two from sample B (MEL.B1, MEL.B2)
evidence: This is supported by genome assembly data in Table 2

claim: Three genomes were recovered from sample C (MEL.C1, MEL.C2, MEL.C3)
source: and three genomes from sample C (MEL.C1, MEL.C2, MEL.C3) for a total of seven distinct genomes reconstructed from human fecal samples
evidence: This is supported by genome assembly data in Table 2

claim: Four complete genomes were established through genome curation
source: Through genome curation, we were able to establish linkage among all scaffolds for four of these genomes (complete genomes; Table 2)
evidence: This is supported by genome assembly data in Table 2

claim: The assembled genomes range from 1.9 to 2.3 Mbp
source: The assembled genomes range from 1.9 to 2.3 Mbp and encode 1,800 to 2,230 genes
evidence: This is supported by genome statistics in Table 2

claim: The assembled genomes encode 1,800 to 2,230 genes
source: The assembled genomes range from 1.9 to 2.3 Mbp and encode 1,800 to 2,230 genes
evidence: This is supported by genome statistics in Table 2

claim: The ACD20 genome is larger than the genomes recovered from fecal samples at 3.0 Mbp encoding 2,819 genes
source: The ACD20 genome is larger than the genomes recovered from fecal samples—3.0 Mbp encoding 2,819 genes
evidence: This is supported by genome statistics in Table 2

claim: A 16S rRNA gene sequence-based phylogeny places the unknown lineages basal to photosynthetic Cyanobacteria
source: Corroborating earlier findings (Ley et al., 2005), a 16S rRNA gene sequence-based phylogeny built with publically available sequences places the unknown lineages, represented in part by the gut and aquifer bacteria, basal to photosynthetic Cyanobacteria (Figure 2A)
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic tree in Figure 2A and citation to Ley et al., 2005

claim: Three subgroups are revealed within the Cyanobacteria-related lineages, one of which comprises sequences obtained from animal guts
source: Three subgroups are revealed, one of which comprises sequences obtained from animal guts (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic tree in Figure 2B

claim: The 16S rRNA gene sequences of the gut and aquifer bacteria share no more than 84% identity to Cyanobacterial sequences
source: The 16S rRNA gene sequences of the gut and aquifer bacteria share no more than 84% identity to Cyanobacterial sequences, consistent with placement of these organisms in a new candidate phylum (<85% identity, as suggested previously [Hugenholtz et al., 1998])
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison data and citation to Hugenholtz et al., 1998

claim: The eight new genomes form a monophyletic lineage that branches deeply from the Cyanobacterial lineage in a concatenated ribosomal protein phylogeny
source: The result shows that the eight new genomes form a monophyletic lineage that branches deeply from the Cyanobacterial lineage, with ACD20 basal to the group (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic tree in Figure 3B

claim: ACD20 is basal to the Melainabacteria group in the concatenated ribosomal protein phylogeny
source: The result shows that the eight new genomes form a monophyletic lineage that branches deeply from the Cyanobacterial lineage, with ACD20 basal to the group (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic tree in Figure 3B

claim: A common ancestor for Melainabacteria and photosynthetic Cyanobacteria is well supported (100/100 bootstrap bipartitions) in both 16S rRNA and ribosomal protein trees
source: Importantly, a common ancestor for these organisms and photosynthetic Cyanobacteria is well supported (100/100 bootstrap bipartitions) in both trees
evidence: This is supported by bootstrap values in the phylogenetic analyses

claim: The melainabacterial genomes contain the 30S ribosomal protein S1 rpsA gene, rather than the homolog ypfD which is exclusive to the Firmicutes
source: For instance, the genomes encode the 30S ribosomal protein S1 rpsA gene, rather than the homolog ypfD, which is exclusive to the Firmicutes (Danchin, 2009)
evidence: This is supported by gene annotation and citation to Danchin, 2009

claim: Two of the gut genomes (MEL.B1 and MEL.B2) encode the A type of RnpB
source: Moreover, two of the gut genomes (MEL.B1 and MEL.B2) encode the A type of RnpB (E-values 5.676e-59, 2.235e-60 respectively), which is found in all Bacteria except the Firmicutes and Tenericutes (Haas et al., 1996; Zwieb et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by gene annotation and citations to Haas et al., 1996 and Zwieb et al., 2011

claim: Three of the four complete genomes have homologs to the S-layer like COG, CyOG00138, a protein found only in Cyanobacteria
source: Three of the four complete genomes also have homologs to the S-layer like COG, CyOG00138 (e.g., Anabaena variabilis: Q3MBT3), a protein found only in Cyanobacteria (Mulkidjanian et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by gene annotation and citation to Mulkidjanian et al., 2006

claim: The Melainabacteria genomes entirely lack genes for photosynthesis
source: The Melainabacteria genomes appear to entirely lack genes for photosynthesis (photosystem I and photosystem II, thylakoid membranes, succinate dehydrogenase, and the cytochrome b6f complex), indicating that none have the capacity for oxygenic or anoxygenic photosynthesis
evidence: This is based on metabolic gene annotation showing absence of photosynthetic genes

claim: Melainabacteria lack genes for soluble and membrane-affiliated electron carrier proteins
source: Also absent are genes for soluble (e.g., plastocyanin or photosynthetic ferredoxin) and membrane-affiliated electron carrier proteins (e.g., cytochromes, quinones, Fe-S, or flavin)
evidence: This is based on metabolic gene annotation

claim: Melainabacteria lack genes for aerobic respiration including terminal quinol and cytochrome c oxidases
source: Additionally, we found no genes for aerobic respiration including terminal quinol and cytochrome c oxidases, terminal reductases involved in anaerobic respiration (e.g., fumarate, nitrate), or carbon fixation pathways
evidence: This is based on metabolic gene annotation

claim: Melainabacteria are not capable of phototrophy or respiratory metabolism
source: Together these findings suggest that these members of the Melainabacteria are not capable of phototrophy or respiratory metabolism
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of genes for photosynthesis and respiration

claim: The melainabacterial genomes encode homologs of the circadian rhythm regulators RpaA and RpaB
source: Despite being non-photosynthetic, the melainabacterial genomes encode homologs of the circadian rhythm regulators RpaA and RpaB and the high intensity light sensor NblS
evidence: This is based on gene annotation

claim: The melainabacterial genomes encode homologs of the high intensity light sensor NblS
source: Despite being non-photosynthetic, the melainabacterial genomes encode homologs of the circadian rhythm regulators RpaA and RpaB and the high intensity light sensor NblS
evidence: This is based on gene annotation

claim: The histidine kinase NblS in Cyanobacteria preserves the photosynthetic machinery by regulating its expression and degradation under high and blue/UV-A conditions
source: The histidine kinase NblS in Cyanobacteria preserves the photosynthetic machinery by regulating its expression and degradation under high and blue/UV-A conditions (van Waasbergen et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citation to van Waasbergen et al., 2002

claim: RpaA and RpaB are found in all Cyanobacteria
source: RpaA and RpaB are found in all Cyanobacteria (Mulkidjanian et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mulkidjanian et al., 2006

claim: RpaA and RpaB regulate the circadian clock KaiABC in Cyanobacteria
source: where they regulate the circadian clock KaiABC (Hanaoka et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hanaoka et al., 2012

claim: RpaA and RpaB link energy transfer between the antennae and the photosystem in Cyanobacteria
source: and link energy transfer between the antennae and the photosystem (Ashby and Mullineaux, 1999)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ashby and Mullineaux, 1999

claim: The four complete genomes of Melainabacteria lack SasA
source: The four complete genomes of Melainabacteria lack SasA, which typically functions as the sensor to the response regulators RpaA and RpaB (Hanaoka et al., 2012)
evidence: This is based on gene annotation and citation to Hanaoka et al., 2012

claim: RpaA and RpaB proteins in Melainabacteria may have a function different from their role in Cyanobacteria
source: as well as any photosynthetic machinery, which suggests that these proteins may have another function
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of photosynthetic machinery in Melainabacteria

claim: The NblS homolog in the gut and aquifer Melainabacteria most likely has a different function than in Cyanobacteria
source: Similarly, the NblS homolog in the gut and aquifer Melainabacteria most likely has a different function
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of photosynthetic machinery in Melainabacteria

claim: RpaA and NblS are exclusive to Cyanobacteria according to the KEGG database
source: The current KEGG database (Kanehisa et al., 2012) indicates that RpaA and NblS are exclusive to Cyanobacteria
evidence: This is based on database information from KEGG

claim: The three Melainabacteria genes RpaA, RpaB, and NblS have highest homology to those present in Cyanobacteria
source: In all cases, the three Melainabacteria genes have highest homology to those present in Cyanobacteria (Supplementary file 1)
evidence: This is based on sequence homology analysis

claim: Melainabacteria are inferred to have a Gram-negative cell envelope
source: Like Cyanobacteria, Melainabacteria are inferred to have a Gram-negative cell envelope
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of genes for LPS, Lipid A, and O-antigen

claim: The curated Melainabacteria genomes contain a large number of genes for lipopolysaccharide (LPS), Lipid A biosynthesis, and O-antigen polymerases and transporters
source: This conclusion is based on the large number of genes for lipopolysaccharide (LPS), Lipid A biosynthesis, and O-antigen polymerases and transporters found in the curated genomes described here (Supplementary file 1)
evidence: This is based on gene annotation

claim: LPS, Lipid A, and O-antigen are components of the Gram-negative outer membrane
source: LPS, Lipid A, and O-antigen are components of the Gram-negative outer membrane; in contrast, Gram-positive bacteria lack an outer membrane and therefore lack these structures (Purves et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Purves et al., 2003 and represents established knowledge

claim: Many genes in the newly reconstructed Melainabacteria genomes share closest sequence similarity to Gram-positive members of the Firmicutes
source: This finding is significant, because many genes in the newly reconstructed genomes share closest sequence similarity to Gram-positive members of the Firmicutes (see below)
evidence: This is based on sequence homology analysis

claim: The Melainabacteria genomes encode a homolog to an S-layer-like protein
source: As previously mentioned, the genomes encode a homolog to an S-layer-like protein, suggesting that the cell envelope has an S-layer
evidence: This is based on gene annotation

claim: S-layers and O-antigens have both been previously observed on photosynthetic Cyanobacteria
source: S-layers and O-antigens have both been previously observed on photosynthetic Cyanobacteria (Hoiczyk and Hansel, 2000)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hoiczyk and Hansel, 2000

claim: Melainabacteria are obligate anaerobic fermenters
source: Based on the lack of a linked electron transport chain, aerobic or anaerobic respiratory complexes (see above), and a complete TCA cycle (see below), and the presence of fermentative and degradative enzymes, we infer that Melainabacteria are obligate anaerobic fermenters
evidence: This is inferred from metabolic gene annotation

claim: Melainabacteria can use a wide variety of carbon compounds including hemicellulosic compounds (only ACD20), polysaccharides, oligosaccharides, and simple sugars
source: We predict that Melainabacteria can use a wide variety of carbon compounds, including hemicellulosic compounds (only ACD20), polysaccharides, oligosaccharides, and simple sugars, as well as organic acids, amino acids, and fatty acids to yield hydrogen, lactate, acetate (ACD20), formate (Gut), hydrogen, possibly butyrate (ACD20) and ethanol (Gut) (Figure 4)
evidence: This is inferred from metabolic gene annotation and shown in Figure 4

claim: Melainabacteria can ferment glucose, fructose, sorbitol, mannose, trehalose, starch, glycogen, hemicellulose, and amylose
source: Specific sugars predicted to be fermented are glucose, fructose, sorbitol, mannose, trehalose, starch, glycogen, hemicellulose, and amylose
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of relevant enzymes

claim: The Melainabacteria genomes encode α-galactosidase, β-galactosidase, α-glucosidase, β-glucosidase, β-glucuronidase, β-fructofranosidase (sucrase), α-mannosidase, pullulanase, α-amylase, and endo-1, 4-beta-xylanase
source: and the relevant enzymes are α-galactosidase, β-galactosidase, α-glucosidase, β-glucosidase, β-glucuronidase, β-fructofranosidase (sucrase), α-mannosidase, pullulanase, α-amylase, and endo-1, 4-beta-xylanase
evidence: This is based on gene annotation

claim: The Melainabacteria genomes contain a pyrophosphate-dependent phosphofructokinase rather than the classical ATP-dependent enzyme
source: This pathway contains not the classical ATP-dependent enzyme, but a pyrophosphate-dependent phosphofructokinase, a gene found in diverse organisms capable of anaerobic glycolysis (Mertens, 1991)
evidence: This is based on gene annotation and citation to Mertens, 1991

claim: The pyrophosphate-dependent phosphofructokinase may confer an energetic advantage when glycolysis is the primary source of ATP
source: This difference in phosphoryl donor specificity may confer an energetic advantage to the cell when glycolysis is the primary source of ATP (Figure 4, gene 3)
evidence: This is inferred from the metabolic context

claim: The Melainabacteria genomes have the genes necessary for hexose interconversion in the EMP pathway via the pentose phosphate pathway
source: The genomes have the genes necessary for hexose interconversion in the EMP pathway via the pentose phosphate pathway, such that ribose, arabinose, xylulose, and other five-carbon sugar or sugar-alcohols may be utilized
evidence: This is based on gene annotation

claim: Unlike most Cyanobacteria, Melainabacteria likely acquire sugars and sugar-alcohols from the environment via cytoplasmic membrane permeases
source: Unlike most Cyanobacteria, which use internal carbon pools for fermentation (Stal and Moezelaar, 1997), Melainabacteria likely acquire sugars and sugar-alcohols from the environment via a variety of cytoplasmic membrane permeases (Figure 4)
evidence: This is inferred from gene annotation and citation to Stal and Moezelaar, 1997

claim: Nearly 30% of the 920 core conserved orthologous genes (COGs) in Melainabacteria match most closely to genes belonging to members of the phylum Firmicutes
source: Nearly 30% of the 920 core conserved orthologous genes (COGs) match most closely to genes belonging to members of the phylum Firmicutes that have a fermentative-based metabolism, compared to 15% with closest matches to cyanobacterial genes (Figure 5A)
evidence: This is based on sequence homology analysis shown in Figure 5A

claim: 15% of the 920 core conserved orthologous genes (COGs) in Melainabacteria have closest matches to cyanobacterial genes
source: Nearly 30% of the 920 core conserved orthologous genes (COGs) match most closely to genes belonging to members of the phylum Firmicutes that have a fermentative-based metabolism, compared to 15% with closest matches to cyanobacterial genes (Figure 5A)
evidence: This is based on sequence homology analysis shown in Figure 5A

claim: Non-cyanobacterial genes in Melainabacteria are spread throughout the genomes
source: These non-cyanobacterial genes are spread throughout the genomes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), arguing against acquisition via a recent lateral transfer event or a chimeric assembly artifact
evidence: This is based on genome organization analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: The COGs whose best match are to COGs of Firmicutes are enriched in functions related to metabolism
source: The COGs whose best match are to COGs of Firmicutes are enriched in functions related to metabolism (Figure 5B), including metabolism of carbohydrates, amino sugars, nucleotides, amino acids, and vitamins
evidence: This is based on functional annotation analysis shown in Figure 5B

claim: Both gut and subsurface Melainabacteria have trimeric confurcating FeFe hydrogenases with motifs required for catalytic activity
source: Both gut and subsurface Melainabacteria studied here have trimeric confurcating FeFe hydrogenases with motifs required for catalytic activity (Figure 4, Supplementary file 1)
evidence: This is based on gene annotation and motif analysis

claim: One of the three confurcating hydrogenases in ACD20 (ACD20_18461) has all the necessary residues for functionality
source: One of the three confurcating hydrogenases in ACD20, ACD20_18461, has all the necessary residues for functionality (L1, L2, and L3 motifs)
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of conserved motifs

claim: The Melainabacteria hydrogenases may indicate an ecological role in H2 production in both gut and subsurface systems
source: These hydrogenases may indicate an ecological role in H2 production in both gut and subsurface systems: syntenic homologs for the three subunits have been identified in genomes of obligate syntrophs and fermenters known to produce high molar ratios of H2 (Sieber et al., 2012)
evidence: This is inferred from comparison to known H2-producing organisms and citation to Sieber et al., 2012

claim: The production of H2 typically requires a syntrophic association with an H2-consuming partner to maintain low partial hydrogen pressures
source: The production of H2 typically requires a syntrophic association with an H2-consuming partner to maintain low partial hydrogen pressures
evidence: This represents established knowledge about H2 metabolism

claim: Melainabacteria may be H2 producers living in syntrophy with archaeal methanogens or bacterial acetogens in the human gut and with respiring organisms in the subsurface
source: Therefore, in addition to being anaerobic fermenters, the Melainabacteria may be H2 producers living in syntrophy with archaeal methanogens or bacterial acetogens in the human gut and with respiring organisms in the subsurface
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of hydrogenases and the requirement for H2-consuming partners

claim: The vast majority of Cyanobacteria have a complete TCA cycle, with Prochlorococcus, marine Synechococcus, and UCYN-A as exceptions
source: With Prochlorococcus, marine Synechococcus, and UCYN-A as exceptions, the vast majority of Cyanobacteria have a complete TCA cycle (Zhang and Bryant, 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang and Bryant, 2011

claim: The Melainabacteria genomes encode no more than four unlinked genes from the TCA and reverse TCA cycles
source: In contrast, the Melainabacteria genomes reported here encode no more than four unlinked genes from the TCA and reverse TCA cycles (Figure 4)
evidence: This is based on metabolic gene annotation shown in Figure 4

claim: The Melainabacteria genomes lack alternative enzymes that functionally complete the TCA cycle in Synechococcus species PCC 7002
source: We also confirmed that the genomes lack alternative enzymes first identified in Synechococcus species PCC 7002 that functionally complete the TCA cycle (Zhang and Bryant, 2011)
evidence: This is based on gene annotation and citation to Zhang and Bryant, 2011

claim: The Melainabacteria genomes have an NAD+ not the NADP+ dependent isocitrate dehydrogenase found in most Cyanobacteria
source: Moreover, the genomes have an NAD+ not the NADP+ dependent isocitrate dehydrogenase found in most Cyanobacteria
evidence: This is based on gene annotation

claim: The absence of a complete TCA cycle necessitates an external requirement for dicarboxylic acids in Melainabacteria
source: The absence of a complete TCA cycle necessitates an external requirement for dicarboxylic acids, which could be imported by the two dicarboxylic acid transporters found in each genome
evidence: This is inferred from the incomplete TCA cycle and presence of transporters

claim: The TCA cycle enzymes in Melainabacteria function to link to nitrogen metabolism and energy generating pathways
source: We infer that the TCA cycle enzymes in the genomes reported here function to link to nitrogen metabolism and energy generating pathways
evidence: This is inferred from metabolic reconstruction

claim: Both the ACD20 and MEL.B2 genomes encode isocitrate dehydrogenase and fumarase
source: Both the ACD20 and MEL.B2 genomes encode isocitrate dehydrogenase and fumarase, whose end-products are important intermediates in nitrogen assimilation and amino acid pathways
evidence: This is based on gene annotation

claim: ACD20 can augment glycolytic ATP substrate-level phosphorylation with additional ATP generation using TCA cycle intermediates
source: Unlike the genomes of the gut bacteria, ACD20 can augment glycolytic ATP substrate-level phosphorylation with additional ATP generation using TCA cycle intermediates
evidence: This is inferred from metabolic reconstruction

claim: ACD20 may use citrate lyase in conjunction with membrane-bound oxaloacetate decarboxylase to pump sodium ions
source: Also, like citrate fermentation in Klebsiella pneuemoniae (Dimroth, 1980; Dimroth and Schink, 1998), ACD20 may use citrate lyase in conjunction with the combined action of membrane-bound oxaloacetate decarboxylase (EC 4.1.1.3) to pump sodium ions
evidence: This is inferred from metabolic reconstruction and citations to Dimroth, 1980 and Dimroth and Schink, 1998

claim: The Melainabacteria can generate a membrane potential by four mechanisms: sodium gradient generation, membrane bound H+-translocating pyrophosphatases, an 11-subunit complex I dehydrogenase, and a putatively annotated six subunit NiFe membrane-bound hydrogenase
source: The Melainabacteria can generate a membrane potential by four mechanisms: (i) a sodium gradient generated by decarboxylation of oxaloacetate (using an oxaloacetate decarboxylase and sodium-hydrogen antiporter, see TCA cycle); (ii) membrane bound H+-translocating pyrophosphatases, which use some of the energy liberated during inorganic pyrophosphate (PPi) hydrolysis to drive proton translocation across the cytoplasmic membrane (Schocke and Schink, 1998); (iii) an 11-subunit complex I dehydrogenase (Battchikova et al., 2011); and (iv) a putatively annotated six subunit NiFe membrane-bound hydrogenase that lacks required hydrogen binding motifs (Vignais and Billoud, 2007; Marreiros et al., 2013)
evidence: This is based on gene annotation and citations to relevant literature

claim: The Melainabacteria genomes lack membrane-associated Rhodobacter nitrogen fixation (Rnf) and formate dehydrogenase complexes
source: Notably, these genomes all lack membrane-associated Rhodobacter nitrogen fixation (Rnf) and formate dehydrogenase complexes found in the genomes of obligate fermentative organisms (McInerney et al., 2007; Biegel et al., 2011)
evidence: This is based on gene annotation and citations to McInerney et al., 2007 and Biegel et al., 2011

claim: The Melainabacteria genomes encode complete pathways for biosynthesis of vitamins B2 (riboflavin), B3 (nicotinamide), B7 (biotin), and B9 (dihydrofolate)
source: The Melainabacteria genomes encode complete pathways for biosynthesis of vitamins B2 (riboflavin), B3 (nicotinamide), B7 (biotin), and B9 (dihydrofolate)
evidence: This is based on metabolic pathway reconstruction

claim: The gut types of Melainabacteria additionally make vitamin B5 (pantoate)
source: The gut types additionally make vitamin B5 (pantoate)
evidence: This is based on metabolic pathway reconstruction

claim: ACD20 and one of the human gut types (MEL.A1) may be able to synthesize vitamins K1 and K2
source: ACD20 and one of the human gut types (MEL.A1) may also be able to synthesize vitamins K1 and K2
evidence: This is based on metabolic pathway reconstruction

claim: Cyanobacteria are capable of synthesizing the B and K vitamins
source: Cyanobacteria are capable of synthesizing the B and K vitamins as well (Kanehisa et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kanehisa et al., 2012

claim: Germ-free animals have an increased nutrient requirement for B and K vitamins, suggesting that the mammalian gut microbiota are a source of these vitamins for the host
source: Germ-free animals raised aseptically, and which lack gut microbiota, have an increased nutrient requirement for B and K vitamins, suggesting that under normal conditions the mammalian gut microbiota are a source of these vitamins for the host (Backhed et al., 2005)

claim: Melainabacteria may represent one of the microbial sources of the B and K vitamins for their hosts
source: Hence, Melainabacteria may represent one of the microbial sources of the B and K vitamins for their hosts
evidence: This is inferred from the vitamin biosynthesis capacity of Melainabacteria

claim: The human gut-derived melainabacterial genomes lack the genes required for a functional nitrogenase complex
source: While the human gut-derived melainabacterial genomes lack the genes required for a functional nitrogenase complex (nifD, nifK, and nifH)
evidence: This is based on gene annotation

claim: The ACD20 genome encodes nifD, nifK, nifH, nifE, nifV, nifS, nifU, nifB, and nifB/X genes involved in nitrogen fixation
source: the ACD20 genome encodes these genes and the nifE, nifV, nifS, nifU, nifB, and nifB/X genes involved in nitrogen fixation
evidence: This is based on gene annotation

claim: The ACD20 NifH protein sequence contains the required [4Fe/4S] cluster, all motifs for functionality, and a conserved lysine in position 15 responsible for ATP interaction
source: We confirmed that the ACD20 NifH protein sequence contains the required [4Fe/4S] cluster, all motifs for functionality, and a conserved lysine in position 15 responsible for ATP interaction
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis

claim: ACD20 likely has the capacity to fix nitrogen
source: Therefore, it seems likely that ACD20 has the capacity to fix nitrogen
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of functional nitrogenase genes

claim: The nifH gene from ACD20 does not cluster with the primary cyanobacterial nifH genes in nifH group I, but is affiliated with nifH group III
source: When placed in phylogenetic context with 865 nifH gene sequences (Zehr et al., 2003), the nifH gene from ACD20 (Figure 6, red) does not cluster with the primary cyanobacterial nifH genes (Figure 6, green) in nifH group I, but is affiliated with nifH group III
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 6 and citation to Zehr et al., 2003

claim: nifH group III is composed of sequences from phylogenetically distant organisms, many of which are obligate anaerobes
source: Group III is composed of sequences from phylogenetically distant organisms, many of which are obligate anaerobes (e.g., Clostridium species, sulfate-reducers, and methanogens) (Zehr et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zehr et al., 2003

claim: The ACD20 nifH sequence was never monophyletic with cyanobacterial sequences in phylogenetic analyses
source: The phylogenetic placement within the nifH cluster III was robust to alignment curation method (manual or automatic with GBLOCKS), and the ACD20 nifH sequence was never monophyletic with cyanobacterial sequences
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis

claim: The best hit to the ACD20 nifH sequence is a group III nitrogenase annotated from Methanoregula boonei 6A8
source: The best hit to the ACD20 nifH sequence is a group III nitrogenase annotated from Methanoregula boonei 6A8 (ABS56522)
evidence: This is based on sequence homology analysis

claim: The melainabacterial nitrogenase is not related to the primary nitrogenase in Cyanobacteria
source: These results indicate that the melainabacterial nitrogenase is not related to the primary nitrogenase in Cyanobacteria
evidence: This is inferred from phylogenetic analysis

claim: The large and small subunit of the glutamine oxoglutarate aminotransferase (GOGAT) system in Melainabacteria are NADP+-based
source: The large and small subunit of the glutamine oxoglutarate aminotransferase (GOGAT) system, responsible for nitrogen assimilation in Melainabacteria, are NADP+-based
evidence: This is based on gene annotation

claim: Cyanobacteria use either a 3Fe-4S ferredoxin-dependent monomeric enzyme or a two subunit NADH-dependent GOGAT
source: This finding distinguishes Melainabacteria from known Cyanobacteria, which use either a 3Fe-4S ferredoxin-dependent monomeric enzyme or a two subunit NADH-dependent GOGAT (Muro-Pastor et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Muro-Pastor et al., 2005

claim: The extant capacity to fix and assimilate nitrogen appears to have been acquired independently in Cyanobacteria and Melainabacteria
source: While a common nitrogenase could have existed in the ancestor of Melainabacteria and Cyanobacteria, the extant capacity to fix and assimilate nitrogen appears to have been acquired independently in Cyanobacteria and this sibling lineage
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distinctness of nitrogenase genes

claim: All four of the analyzed Melainabacteria genomes contain genes for flagella production
source: All four of the analyzed genomes contain genes for flagella production, and all but one of the analyzed gut genomes (MEL.A1) contains the requisite genes to produce a fully functional flagellum (Supplementary file 1)
evidence: This is based on gene annotation

claim: All but one of the analyzed gut genomes (MEL.A1) contains the requisite genes to produce a fully functional flagellum
source: All four of the analyzed genomes contain genes for flagella production, and all but one of the analyzed gut genomes (MEL.A1) contains the requisite genes to produce a fully functional flagellum (Supplementary file 1)
evidence: This is based on gene annotation

claim: The flagella in Melainabacteria are composed of the M, S, P, and L rings, as expected given a Gram-negative cell envelope
source: The flagella are composed of the M, S, P, and L rings, as expected given a Gram-negative cell envelope (DePamphilis and Adler, 1971)
evidence: This is based on gene annotation and citation to DePamphilis and Adler, 1971

claim: At least one copy of the flagellin protein in each Melainabacteria genome contains the eight amino acid sequence recognized by Toll-like receptor 5
source: At least one copy of the flagellin protein in each Melainabacteria genome contains the eight amino acid sequence recognized by Toll-like receptor 5 (Andersen-Nissen et al., 2005), indicating an ability to interact with the host immune system (Figure 7)
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 7 and citation to Andersen-Nissen et al., 2005

claim: Trees built using flagellum-related gene sequences show that the genes branch deeply with the Firmicutes and Spirochaetes
source: Trees built using flagellum-related gene sequences show that the genes branch deeply with the Firmicutes and Spirochaetes (Figure 8), arguably the two most basal bacterial lineages (Daubin et al., 2002; Ciccarelli et al., 2006)
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 8 and citations to Daubin et al., 2002 and Ciccarelli et al., 2006

claim: The common ancestor of Cyanobacteria and Melainabacteria may have been flagellated
source: This result suggests that the common ancestor of Cyanobacteria and Melainabacteria may have been flagellated
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic placement of flagellar genes

claim: No flagellated Cyanobacteria are known
source: Given that no flagellated Cyanobacteria are known and cyanobacterial motility is accomplished by gliding or twitching (Schaechter, 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schaechter, 2010

claim: Cyanobacterial motility is accomplished by gliding or twitching
source: Given that no flagellated Cyanobacteria are known and cyanobacterial motility is accomplished by gliding or twitching (Schaechter, 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schaechter, 2010

claim: Flagella may have been non-essential to the cyanobacterial lifestyle and hence lost
source: flagella may have been non-essential to the cyanobacterial lifestyle and hence lost
evidence: This is speculation about evolutionary history

claim: The gut–associated clade of the Melainabacteria appears to have undergone genome reduction relative to ACD20
source: The gut–associated clade of the Melainabacteria, which diverged from the sediment-associated lineage, appears to have undergone genome reduction relative to ACD20 (Figure 3, Table 2)
evidence: This is inferred from genome size comparisons shown in Figure 3 and Table 2

claim: The gut types of Melainabacteria lack genes for chemotaxis
source: The gut types lack genes for chemotaxis, production of some amino acids (aspartic acid, asparagine, phenylalanine, arginine, histidine, tyrosine, and, in MEL.A1 and MEL.B1, alanine), a type I secretion system, nitrogen fixation, and genes for additional energy generation by substrate-level phosphorylation and for the production of acetate and perhaps butyrate as fermentation end-products
evidence: This is based on gene annotation

claim: Genome reduction has been observed in symbiotic bacteria and may have occurred in Melainabacteria during adaptation to life in the animal gut
source: Genome reduction has been observed in symbiotic bacteria and may have occurred in Melainabacteria during adaptation to life in the animal gut
evidence: This is inferred from genome size comparisons and represents a hypothesis

claim: The lack of flagellum biosynthesis genes in MEL.A1 indicates that these genes were likely not missed in the genome sequencing and assembly but rather that further genome reduction may be ongoing
source: The lack of the filament, filament cap, hook-filament junction, and L and P rings required for flagellum biosynthesis in the genome assembled into a single scaffold (MEL.A1) indicates that these genes were likely not missed in the genome sequencing and assembly but rather that further genome reduction may be ongoing in the gut-associated clade
evidence: This is inferred from the completeness of the MEL.A1 genome assembly

claim: The water-soil-sediment (non-animal associated) clade of Melainabacteria was detected in a wide variety of environments, with the highest abundances in municipal water
source: We detected the water-soil-sediment (non-animal associated) clade in a wide variety of environments (Figure 9), with the highest abundances in municipal water
evidence: This is based on 16S rRNA gene survey data shown in Figure 9

claim: Melainabacteria occur as rare members of skin, airway, and mouth communities across the human body
source: An analysis of the Human Microbiome Project (Consortium HMP, 2012) and other datasets (Figure 9—source data 1) showed that across the human body, they occur as rare members of skin, airway, and mouth communities, but are most abundant in fecal samples (Figure 9B)
evidence: This is based on analysis of HMP data shown in Figure 9B

claim: Melainabacteria are most abundant in fecal samples across the human body
source: An analysis of the Human Microbiome Project (Consortium HMP, 2012) and other datasets (Figure 9—source data 1) showed that across the human body, they occur as rare members of skin, airway, and mouth communities, but are most abundant in fecal samples (Figure 9B)
evidence: This is based on analysis of HMP data shown in Figure 9B

claim: The gut types of Melainabacteria were detected in fecal samples from a range of mammalian species, with the highest levels in herbivores
source: The gut types were also detected in fecal samples from a range of other mammalian species, with the highest levels in herbivores, consistent with a role in fermentation of dietary substrates (Figure 9C)
evidence: This is based on 16S rRNA gene survey data shown in Figure 9C

claim: Melainabacteria are more abundant in feces obtained from foregut than hindgut fermenters within herbivores
source: Within the herbivores, Melainabacteria are more abundant in feces obtained from foregut than hindgut fermenters (two tailed t-test, p=0.026)
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of 16S rRNA gene survey data

claim: Approximately 10% of samples in the Human Microbiome Project dataset contained melainabacterial 16S rRNA gene sequences
source: Within the Human Microbiome Project dataset (Consortium HMP, 2012), approximately 10% of the samples contained melainabacterial 16S rRNA gene sequences, providing a rough estimate as to what fraction of the American population carries Melainabacteria
evidence: This is based on analysis of HMP data

claim: The highest abundances of Melainabacteria in humans were observed in fecal samples obtained from predominantly vegetarian Malawian and Venezuelan individuals
source: When comparing three global human populations (Yatsunenko et al., 2012), we observed the highest abundances in fecal samples obtained from predominantly vegetarian Malawian and Venezuelan individuals (Figure 9C)
evidence: This is based on analysis of data from Yatsunenko et al., 2012 shown in Figure 9C

claim: Melainabacteria play a role in fermentation of dietary plant polysaccharides in humans
source: These observations suggest that Melainabacteria also play a role in fermentation of dietary plant polysaccharides in humans
evidence: This is inferred from the distribution patterns in vegetarian populations

claim: High throughput sequencing and bioinformatic methods enabled recovery of four complete and four partial genomes for relatively rare members of complex microbial communities
source: High throughput sequencing and bioinformatic methods enabled recovery of four complete and four partial genomes for relatively rare members of complex microbial communities from the adult human gut and groundwater
evidence: This summarizes the methodological achievement of the study

claim: The approach used can yield complete genomes from relatively low abundance organisms, without the need for single cell genomic approaches
source: We show that these methods can yield complete and near-complete genomes from relatively low abundance organisms, without the need for single cell genomic approaches
evidence: This is based on the successful genome recovery from low abundance organisms

claim: Recovery of complete genomes was facilitated by the uniqueness of the Melainabacteria genomes
source: Recovery of complete genomes was facilitated by the uniqueness of the Melainabacteria genomes, which were distinct not only from the genomes of all other organisms in the community but also were differentiable among coexisting Melainabacteria
evidence: This explains the methodological success

claim: The metagenomic approach has the potential to replace culture-based, single cell, and flow cytometry-based genomics methods
source: This approach has the potential to replace culture-based, single cell, and flow cytometry-based genomics methods, which are costlier and more laborious due to the requirement for cell manipulation
evidence: This is a claim about the methodological implications

claim: The amplification step in single cell genomics often results in partial genomes
source: Moreover, the amplification step in single cell genomics often results in partial genomes (Marcy et al., 2007; Podar et al., 2007; Youssef et al., 2011) and chimeras (Zhang et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Marcy et al., 2007; Podar et al., 2007; Youssef et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2006

claim: Novel bacterial 16S rRNA sequences have traditionally been assigned to new candidate phyla based on low levels of sequence identity to existing phyla
source: Traditionally, novel bacterial 16S rRNA sequences have been assigned to new candidate phyla based on low levels of sequence identity to existing phyla, and use of this criterion supports the assignment of these bacteria to a new phylum distinct from Cyanobacteria (Hugenholtz et al., 1998)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hugenholtz et al., 1998

claim: Sequences previously referred to as deep branching Cyanobacteria, YS2, SM1D11, or mle1-12 should be reclassified to the candidate phylum Melainabacteria
source: here we suggest reclassification of sequences previously referred to as deep branching Cyanobacteria, YS2, SM1D11, or mle1-12 to the candidate phylum Melainabacteria
evidence: This is a taxonomic proposal based on phylogenetic analysis

claim: ACD20 should be assigned to the Melainabacteria candidate phylum
source: Similarly, ACD20 should be assigned to the Melainabacteria candidate phylum
evidence: This is a taxonomic proposal based on phylogenetic analysis

claim: Melainabacteria are not only important members of the human gut but their unique evolutionary placement also provides novel insight into the evolution of Cyanobacteria
source: Melainabacteria are, therefore, not only important members of the human gut but their unique evolutionary placement also provides novel insight into the evolution of Cyanobacteria
evidence: This summarizes the significance of the findings

claim: Melainabacteria are anaerobic, obligate fermenters capable of utilizing diverse carbon sources
source: Our metabolic reconstruction indicates that the Melainabacteria are anaerobic, obligate fermenters capable of utilizing diverse carbon sources, which are imported as well as derived from internal carbon sources
evidence: This is based on metabolic reconstruction from genomic data

claim: Melainabacteria lack a linked electron transport chain but have multiple methods for generating a membrane potential
source: Melainabacteria lack a linked electron transport chain but have multiple methods for generating a membrane potential, which can then produce ATP via an ATP synthase
evidence: This is based on metabolic reconstruction from genomic data

claim: Melainabacteria use FeFe hydrogenases for H2 production, distinct from Cyanobacteria which have NiFe hydrogenases
source: Distinct from Cyanobacteria (which have NiFe hydrogenases [Tamagnini et al., 2007]), the Melainabacteria cells use FeFe hydrogenases for H2 production and may require an H2-sink (e.g., a coexisting acetogen, methanogen, or other respiring partner) to maintain low partial H2 pressures
evidence: This is based on gene annotation and citation to Tamagnini et al., 2007

claim: Efforts to culture Melainabacteria should focus on providing a diverse array of sugars and carbohydrates, dicarboxylic acids, and a complete set of amino acids in an anaerobic, dark environment
source: Efforts to culture Melainabacteria should focus on providing a diverse array of sugars and carbohydrates, dicarboxylic acids, and a complete set of amino acids in an anaerobic, dark environment
evidence: This is inferred from the metabolic reconstruction

claim: Culturing strategies for Melainabacteria should include removal of hydrogen through use of an H2-consuming syntrophic partner
source: Moreover, given their production of H2, these strategies should include removal of hydrogen through use of an H2-consuming syntrophic partner
evidence: This is inferred from the metabolic reconstruction

claim: The protein sequences of the flagellin genes of Melainabacteria are recognized by Toll-like receptor 5
source: We infer that the protein sequences of the flagellin genes of Melainabacteria are recognized by Toll-like receptor 5 (as are flagellins of some commensal Firmicutes in the mammalian gut) that mediates interaction with the host
evidence: This is inferred from sequence analysis of flagellin proteins

claim: The human gut Melainabacteria may provide their host with B and K vitamins and fill a niche based on carbon fermentation in the large intestine
source: The human gut Melainabacteria may provide their host with B and K vitamins and fill a niche based on carbon fermentation in the large intestine, analogous to that of the Firmicutes
evidence: This is inferred from metabolic reconstruction and distribution patterns

claim: The gut Melainabacteria flourish in the presence of plant polysaccharides and may aid in the digestion of plant fibers
source: Based on their distribution in animals and humans living on different continents and consuming different diets, we hypothesize that the gut Melainabacteria flourish in the presence of plant polysaccharides and may aid in the digestion of plant fibers
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on distribution patterns in vegetarian populations

claim: Oxygenic photosynthesis did not arise prior to the divergence of Melainabacteria from Cyanobacteria
source: We infer that this capacity did not arise prior to the divergence of Melainabacteria from Cyanobacteria, based on the absence of remnants of photosynthetic machinery in the Melainabacteria genomes
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of photosynthetic genes in Melainabacteria

claim: UCYN-A is the sole representative of Cyanobacteria unable to perform oxygenic photosynthesis due to loss of photosystem II
source: This observation is in contrast to the symbiotic photoheterotroph UCYN-A, which is the sole representative of Cyanobacteria unable to perform oxygenic photosynthesis due to loss of photosystem II (Tripp et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tripp et al., 2010

claim: A similar loss of photosynthesis appears to have occurred in the nitrogen-fixing endosymbiont of the algae Rhopalodia gibba
source: A similar loss of photosynthesis appears to have occurred in the nitrogen-fixing endosymbiont of the algae Rhopalodia gibba (Kneip et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kneip et al., 2008

claim: The cyanobacterial ability to sense and use light was preceded and perhaps facilitated by response regulator systems present in the proto-Cyanobacteria
source: The presence of a light stress response regulator (NblS) and circadian rhythm regulator (RpaA and RpaB) homologs in this sibling phylum suggests that the cyanobacterial ability to sense and use light was preceded and perhaps facilitated by response regulator systems present in the proto-Cyanobacteria
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of light response regulators in Melainabacteria

claim: Acquisition of nitrogen fixation occurred after Cyanobacteria and Melainabacteria diverged
source: Like Cyanobacteria, the subsurface Melainabacteria (ACD20) is capable of nitrogen fixation but its nitrogenase genes appear to be unrelated. Though we cannot rule out the existence of an ancient nitrogenase common in both lineages, this finding suggests that acquisition of nitrogen fixation occurred after Cyanobacteria and Melainabacteria diverged
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distinctness of nitrogenase genes

claim: The sequence of events placing photosynthesis before nitrogen fixation is in agreement with other theories
source: This sequence of events is in agreement with other theories, which place the development of photosynthesis before nitrogen fixation (Sanchez-Baracaldo et al., 2005; Shi and Falkowski, 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sanchez-Baracaldo et al., 2005 and Shi and Falkowski, 2008

claim: Cyanobacteria gained the capacities for oxygenic photosynthesis and nitrogen fixation and lost or never gained flagella after diverging from Melainabacteria
source: Thus, we speculate that Cyanobacteria gained the capacities for oxygenic photosynthesis and nitrogen fixation and lost or never gained flagella after diverging from Melainabacteria
evidence: This is speculation based on comparative genomics

claim: Melainabacteria gained or maintained flagella, a fermentation system, and an array of carbon transporters
source: Melainabacteria on the other hand, gained or maintained flagella, a fermentation system, and an array of carbon transporters
evidence: This is inferred from comparative genomics

claim: One environmental (non-gut) lineage of Melainabacteria acquired nitrogen fixation, whereas the gut lineage capitalized on its ability to ferment diverse carbon sources
source: One environmental (non-gut) lineage of Melainabacteria acquired nitrogen fixation, whereas the gut lineage capitalized on its ability to ferment diverse carbon sources, including those recalcitrant to host digestion
evidence: This is inferred from comparative genomics and distribution patterns

claim: The common ancestors of Cyanobacteria and Melainabacteria may have been Gram-negative flagellated bacteria active in the anaerobic carbon cycle, producing H2, but not fixing nitrogen
source: We conclude that the common ancestors of Cyanobacteria and Melainabacteria may have been Gram-negative flagellated bacteria active in the anaerobic carbon cycle, producing H2, but not fixing nitrogen
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparative genomics and phylogenetic analysis

claim: The characterization of the common ancestor is consistent with the idea that the ancestors of Cyanobacteria were anoxygenic photosynthetic organisms with a photosystem I-like reaction center
source: Although this characterization does not clarify the origins of photosynthesis, it is consistent with the idea that the ancestors of Cyanobacteria were anoxygenic photosynthetic organisms with a photosystem I-like reaction center (Mulkidjanian et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mulkidjanian et al., 2006

claim: The inferred lifestyle is consistent with the hypothesis that the common ancestor of extant bacteria relied on anaerobic decomposition of organic material by substrate-level phosphorylation
source: The inferred lifestyle is consistent with the widely accepted hypothesis that the common ancestor of extant bacteria relied on anaerobic decomposition of organic material by substrate-level phosphorylation (Egami, 1977) and was likely metabolically similar to the Firmicutes (Daubin et al., 2002; Ciccarelli et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Egami, 1977; Daubin et al., 2002; Ciccarelli et al., 2006

claim: The reconstruction of genomes from uncultivated bacteria has enabled description of Melainabacteria and further elucidation of the evolutionary history of Cyanobacteria
source: The reconstruction of genomes from uncultivated bacteria from human gut and subsurface environmental metagenomes has enabled us to describe Melainabacteria, a novel candidate phylum sibling to Cyanobacteria, and to further elucidate the evolutionary history of one of the Earth's most important bacterial phyla
evidence: This summarizes the main achievement of the study

claim: Photosynthesis probably developed in Cyanobacteria after the separation from Melainabacteria
source: Our results suggest that while photosynthesis probably developed in Cyanobacteria after the separation from Melainabacteria, the evolution of light related capabilities may have been enabled by regulators present in their common ancestor
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of photosynthetic genes in Melainabacteria

claim: The evolution of light related capabilities may have been enabled by regulators present in the common ancestor of Cyanobacteria and Melainabacteria
source: Our results suggest that while photosynthesis probably developed in Cyanobacteria after the separation from Melainabacteria, the evolution of light related capabilities may have been enabled by regulators present in their common ancestor
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of light response regulators in Melainabacteria

claim: The ability to fix nitrogen appears to have developed separately in Cyanobacteria and the water-soil-sediment clade of Melainabacteria
source: The ability to fix nitrogen appears to have developed separately in Cyanobacteria and the water-soil-sediment clade of Melainabacteria
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distinctness of nitrogenase genes

claim: The role of the Melainabacteria in the human gut is one of an obligate fermenter
source: The role of the Melainabacteria in the human gut is one of an obligate fermenter, and its enrichment in human subjects and animals with a plant-rich diet likely relates to a prominent role of the Melainabacteria in the processing of plant fibers
evidence: This is inferred from metabolic reconstruction and distribution patterns

claim: The enrichment of Melainabacteria in human subjects and animals with a plant-rich diet likely relates to a prominent role in the processing of plant fibers
source: The role of the Melainabacteria in the human gut is one of an obligate fermenter, and its enrichment in human subjects and animals with a plant-rich diet likely relates to a prominent role of the Melainabacteria in the processing of plant fibers
evidence: This is inferred from distribution patterns in vegetarian populations

claim: As plant fibers have been minimized in Western diets, the Melainabacteria may be regarded as part of the microbiota that is disappearing from modernized populations
source: As plant fibers have been minimized in Western diets, the Melainabacteria may be regarded as part of the microbiota that is disappearing from modernized populations (Blaser and Falkow, 2009)
evidence: This is speculation based on distribution patterns and citation to Blaser and Falkow, 2009

claim: The metabolic reconstructions made from these genomes should guide efforts into obtaining Melainabacteria in culture
source: The metabolic reconstructions made from these genomes should guide efforts into obtaining Melainabacteria in culture, which would allow a better understanding of this important human symbiont
evidence: This is a prospective statement about future research
